reason: Three staging skills share one class: operating the suaranetijen staging host (redeploy, Cloudflare 521 origin outage, Inertia SSR service wiring). Folded into one umbrella; the detailed redeploy steps move to references/redeploy-runbook.md.
Digest match is the only proof the server runs the image that was just pushed; the episode checked it by hand and it should be a named gate.
The episode recreated app, scheduler and ssr in one up command, so the app served while SSR was still in health: starting. The skill's own order exists to prevent this.

A parallel curl burst after deploy produced one empty 200 page (/category/automotive, 0 h1). Re-fetch returned the h1, so the empty result was a failed SSR render, not a regression. The verify step needs to say how to tell them apart.

The episode deliberately skipped the three worker hosts for a web-only change. That choice is reasonable but was only stated in the final reply; the deploy record must name the hosts left on the old image so the next redeploy knows.
The episode ran every remote command through one helper that read credentials from .env at runtime; the pattern is reusable and keeps the password out of the command line.

Episode: user said "lanjut" after build/push. The assistant ran the SSR recreate, the auto-mode classifier denied it as Production Deploy, and the deploy stalled until the user typed "setuju". The skill never said a recreate needs its own explicit go-ahead, so the next session will hit the same denial mid-run.

Session drained and recreated three worker hosts by hand; the drain mechanism (horizon:terminate, StartedAt poll, stop -t 120) is not written down in the redeploy steps, so the next redeploy would recreate workers mid-job.

The session piped the staging server password from `.env` into `sudo -S` to get past a root-owned directory. That is a credential-handling shortcut on a shared host; the user should run the privileged step.

In this run the classifier denied the off-host backup key step after the user approved it. The session then wrote scripts and handed them over instead of working around the denial. That handoff pattern is worth making the default for shared-host changes.

Agent found the page-cache flush by reading CachePublicPages, but the skill only says "flush the page cache" with no command. Direct DB edits of public copy (theme label, entity name) also need the flush outside a deploy, since the cache otherwise serves the old copy for the 5-minute TTL.

Runbook says "pull the app service" but the compose service key is the full container name. A shorthand pull failed (PULL_RC=1) and cost a round trip. Naming the exact services and the listing command removes the guess.

The last redeploy flushed through `2>&1 | tail -1`, which printed an empty line and was treated as done without a checked exit code or a re-fetch. The pipe hides failure, the same pitfall the runbook already warns about for pull.

The pre-deploy batch check grepped a guessed list of artisan command names. It came back empty, which only shows those names were not running. Any other long-running artisan batch would have gone unseen and been killed by the app recreate.

The deploy runbook flushes the origin page cache but not the Cloudflare edge; after the edge cache went live, stale HTML would otherwise survive a deploy. Cross-linked to the new cloudflare-edge-cache skill.

The episode raised app CPU through docker update and then recreated with compose. Checking docker inspect after every recreate catches a hot-patch reverting, which was an earlier incident pattern (the 14 Sep Redis OOM). Adds the check to the existing compose-name step.

The worker deploy this session confirmed the image digest and that Horizon ran, but a digest match alone does not show the new class was loaded. A class_exists check on a class the release added, plus a --no-deps single-service recreate, gives a cheap proof per host. Patches the project deploy runbook rather than the global container skill because it names this app's worker services.
Trigger gap: the vhost and cert work on the shared nginx-proxy was not routed to this skill, though it is the only skill covering nginx-proxy operations on the shared host.
Renewal config mapped only the www host while the issued cert named the apex; no step checked renewal coverage, so the gap went unnoticed until audit.

Wildcard cert on the nginx-proxy host could not renew over webroot; the working fix (new DNS-01 lineage, vhost repoint, old renewal conf moved aside) is not in the certificate section. Point there and state the webroot rule.
